---
title: "The equivalence between DFAs and NFAs"
bibliography: ../../formal_complexity.bib
---

It turns out that DFAs and NFAs are equivalent, in the sense that they characterize the same set of languages---the regular languages.
Not only that, but it is possible to convert between them:
there is a systematic procedure for turning any random DFA into an NFA, as well as one for turning any NFA into a DFA.^[
	The translation from NFAs to DFAs defined here is based on @white_two_2026.
]

To show this, we first provide the following alternative definition of NFAs, which is equivalent to the definition provided by @partee_mathematical_1990.
According to this definition, $K$, $Σ$, $q_{0}$, and $F$ remain the same, but we present the transition relation slightly differently.
Instead of a relation
$$Δ ⊆ (K × Σ^{*}) × K$$
we define a function 
$$Δ : K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}) → 2^{K}$$
That is, $Δ$ is defined instead as a function that takes pairs of (1) states, and (2) either elements of the alphabet or $ϵ$, onto *sets of new states*.

Note that any such function is equivalent to a relation on $K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\})$ and $K$:
given such a function $Δ$, you can simply define the relation
$$R = \{⟨q, x, q′⟩ ∣ q′ ∈ Δ(q, x)\}$$
Note that if $Δ(q, x) = \varnothing$ for some $q ∈ K$ and $x ∈ Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}$, then $q$ and $x$ aren't related to any output state by the relation $R$.

Meanwhile, if you have a relation $R ⊆ (K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\})) × K$, you can simply define the function
$$Δ(q, x) = \{q′ ∈ K ∣ ⟨q, x, q′⟩ ∈ R\}$$
Note (correspondingly) that for any $q ∈ K$ and $x ∈ Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}$, if $R$ doesn't relate $q$ and $x$ to any output state, then $Δ(q, x) = \varnothing$.

## Example

Consider the language discussed in [the example from earlier](nfas.html#example).
That is, $L = \{ac, abc, bc\}$.
Using the alternative definition, we can provide the following NFA characterizing this language.

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 1.8

digraph NFA {
  rankdir=LR;

  graph [
    margin=0,
    pad=0,
    splines=true,
    nodesep=0.5,
    ranksep=0.55
  ];

  node [
    shape=circle,
    width=0.45,
    height=0.45,
    fontsize=10
  ];

  edge [
    fontsize=10,
    arrowsize=0.25
  ];

  start [
    shape=none,
    label="",
    width=0,
    height=0,
    margin=0
  ];

  q0 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>0</I></SUB>>];
  qa [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>a</I></SUB>>];
  qb [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>b</I></SUB>>];
  q1 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>1</I></SUB>>, shape=doublecircle];

  start:e -> q0:w;

  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>ϵ</I>>];

  q0 -> qb [label=<<I>a</I>>];

  qa -> qb [label=<<I>b</I>>];

  qb -> q1 [label=<<I>c</I>>];
}
```

- $K = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}, q_{1}\}$
- $Σ = \{a, b, c\}$
- $F = \{q_{1}\}$
- $Δ(q_{0}, a) = \{q_{a}, q_{b}\}$ <br> $Δ(q_{0}, b) = Δ(q_{0}, c) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{0}, ϵ) = \{q_{a}\}$ <br> 
  $Δ(q_{a}, a) = Δ(q_{a}, c) = Δ(q_{a}, ϵ) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{a}, b) = \{q_{b}\}$ <br>
  $Δ(q_{b}, a) = Δ(q_{b}, b) = Δ(q_{b}, ϵ) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{b}, c) = \{q_{1}\}$ <br>
  $Δ(q_{1}, a) = Δ(q_{1}, b) = Δ(q_{1}, c) = Δ(q_{1}, ϵ) = \varnothing$

## Translating DFAs into NFAs

To show that any DFA yields an equivalent NFA, one need only adjust its transition function $δ$ so that it instead maps pairs of states and words of the alphabet onto *sets* of output states.
Given a word $w$ and state $q$, which set of states should the pair $⟨q, w⟩$ be mapped to?
Simply, the one-element set $\{δ(q, w)\}$, whatever that is.

Thus given a DFA $⟨K, Σ, δ, q_{0}, F⟩$, we can define the NFA $⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩$, where $Δ(q, w) = \{δ(q, w)\}$ and $Δ(q, ϵ) = \varnothing$ (for any $q$).
In a sense, every DFA already is an NFA;
we are just rearranging the definition slightly.

## Translating NFAs into DFAs

Going the other direction is more interesting.
To do this, there are a couple of definitions it is useful to provide.

### $ϵ$-only paths

First, we need the notion of a finite $ϵ$-only path.
Given some NFA, a finite $ϵ$-only path can be viewed as a sequence of transitions (possibly of length 0) through its state diagram which only involve $ϵ$.
In the state diagram above, for instance, there is exactly one finite $ϵ$-only path of length at least 1 (every state has a length-0 $ϵ$-only path to itself):
the one from $q_{0}$ to $q_{a}$.
By contrast, consider the following state diagram:

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 1.8

digraph NFA {
  rankdir=LR;

  graph [
    margin=0,
    pad=0,
    splines=true,
    nodesep=0.5,
    ranksep=0.55
  ];

  node [
    shape=circle,
    width=0.45,
    height=0.45,
    fontsize=10
  ];

  edge [
    fontsize=10,
    arrowsize=0.25
  ];

  start [
    shape=none,
    label="",
    width=0,
    height=0,
    margin=0
  ];

  q0 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>0</I></SUB>>];
  qa [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>a</I></SUB>>];
  qb [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>b</I></SUB>>];
  q1 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>1</I></SUB>>, shape=doublecircle];

  start:e -> q0:w;

  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>ϵ</I>>];

  q0 -> qb [label=<<I>a</I>>];

  qa -> qb [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  qa -> qb [label=<<I>ϵ</I>>];

  qb -> q1 [label=<<I>c</I>>];
}
```
The NFA represented by this state diagram has three finite $ϵ$-only paths of length at least 1 (again, every state has a length-0 $ϵ$-only path to itself):
one from $q_{0}$ to $q_{a}$;
one from $q_{a}$ to $q_{b}$;
and one from $q_{0}$ to $q_{b}$.
The last path comes from sequencing the first two paths.

More formally, given the transition function $Δ : K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}) → 2^{K}$, we can define a relation $Δ_{ϵ} ⊆ K × K$:
$$Δ_{ϵ} ≝ \{⟨q, q′⟩ ∣ q′ ∈ Δ(q, ϵ)\}$$
That is, $Δ_{ϵ}$ relates $q$ to $q′$ just in case you can reach $q′$ from $q$ in one step by reading an $ϵ$.

Let us now define the notion of *composing $Δ_{ϵ}$ with itself* an arbitrary number of times, denoted $Δ_{ϵ}^{n}$ (where $n$ is the relevant "arbitrary" number).
$$Δ_{ϵ}^{0} ≝ \{⟨q, q⟩ ∣ q ∈ K\}$$
$$Δ_{ϵ}^{n+1} ≝ Δ_{ϵ} ∘ Δ_{ϵ}^{n}$$
Thus $Δ_{ϵ}^{0}$ is the identity relation on $K$;
$Δ_{ϵ}^{1}$ is just $Δ_{ϵ}$ itself;
$Δ_{ϵ}^{2}$ is $Δ_{ϵ} ∘ Δ_{ϵ}$ (i.e., $Δ_{ϵ}$ composed with itself);
and so on.
Then the following relation, $Δ_{ϵ}^{*}$, is known as the *reflexive transitive closure* of the relation $Δ_{ϵ}$:
$$Δ_{ϵ}^{*} ≝ ⋃_{i ∈ ℕ}Δ_{ϵ}^{i}$$
In words, $Δ_{ϵ}^{*}$ relates two states $q$ and $q′$ just in case there is a finite (possibly length-0) $ϵ$-only path from $q$ to $q′$ in the state diagram of the NFA whose transition function is $Δ$.
Because length-0 paths are also allowed, the relation is *reflexive*;
i.e., it relates any state in $K$ (the set of states) to itself.

### ϵ-closure by finite paths

For any set of states $Q ⊆ K$, we can define its *epsilon closure by finite paths* $Ε(Q)$:
$$Ε(Q) ≝ \{q′ ∣ \text{there is some } q \text{ in } Q \text{, and } ⟨q, q′⟩ ∈ Δ_{ϵ}^{*}\}$$
In words, given any set $Q$ of states, $Ε(Q)$ has as an element every state in $Q$ itself, as well as every state you can get to from a state in $Q$ via a finite $ϵ$-only path.

Consider again the state diagram given just above, and consider the set $\{q_{0}\}$.
Then, $Ε(\{q_{0}\}) = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}\}$;
this is the set of states reachable from $q_{0}$ by some finite $ϵ$-only path.
Note that if we instead consider the set $\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}$, we get the same set again:
$Ε(\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}) = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}\}$.

### The translation

We can now straightforwardly define the translation from an arbitrary NFA to its DFA which accepts the same language.
Given an NFA $⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩$, we define the corresponding DFA $⟨K′, Σ′, δ, q_{0}′, F′⟩$ as follows.

- $K′ = 2^{K}$
- $Σ′ = Σ$
- $δ(Q, w) = Ε(⋃_{q ∈ Q}Δ(q, w))$ (where $w ∈ Σ$)
- $q_{0}′ = Ε(\{q_{0}\})$
- $F′ = \{Q ∣ Q ∩ F ≠ \varnothing\}$

## Example

Consider our original example of an NFA again, repeated here.

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 1.8

digraph NFA {
  rankdir=LR;

  graph [
    margin=0,
    pad=0,
    splines=true,
    nodesep=0.5,
    ranksep=0.55
  ];

  node [
    shape=circle,
    width=0.45,
    height=0.45,
    fontsize=10
  ];

  edge [
    fontsize=10,
    arrowsize=0.25
  ];

  start [
    shape=none,
    label="",
    width=0,
    height=0,
    margin=0
  ];

  q0 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>0</I></SUB>>];
  qa [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>a</I></SUB>>];
  qb [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>b</I></SUB>>];
  q1 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB><I>1</I></SUB>>, shape=doublecircle];

  start:e -> q0:w;

  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  q0 -> qa [label=<<I>ϵ</I>>];

  q0 -> qb [label=<<I>a</I>>];

  qa -> qb [label=<<I>b</I>>];

  qb -> q1 [label=<<I>c</I>>];
}
```

- $K = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}, q_{1}\}$
- $Σ = \{a, b, c\}$
- $F = \{q_{1}\}$
- $Δ(q_{0}, a) = \{q_{a}, q_{b}\}$ <br> $Δ(q_{0}, b) = Δ(q_{0}, c) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{0}, ϵ) = \{q_{a}\}$ <br> 
  $Δ(q_{a}, a) = Δ(q_{a}, c) = Δ(q_{a}, ϵ) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{a}, b) = \{q_{b}\}$ <br>
  $Δ(q_{b}, a) = Δ(q_{b}, b) = Δ(q_{b}, ϵ) = \varnothing$ <br> $Δ(q_{b}, c) = \{q_{1}\}$ <br>
  $Δ(q_{1}, a) = Δ(q_{1}, b) = Δ(q_{1}, c) = Δ(q_{1}, ϵ) = \varnothing$

By using the translation procedure defined above, we obtain the following DFA.

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 6
//| fig-height: 3

digraph DFA {
  rankdir=LR;

  graph [
    margin=0,
    pad=0,
    splines=true,
    nodesep=0.55,
    ranksep=0.7
  ];

  node [
    shape=circle,
    fontsize=10
  ];

  edge [
    fontsize=10,
    arrowsize=0.25
  ];

  start [
    shape=none,
    label="",
    width=0,
    height=0,
    margin=0
  ];

  q0a [
    label=<{<I>q</I><SUB><I>0</I></SUB>, <I>q</I><SUB><I>a</I></SUB>}>
  ];

  qab [
    label=<{<I>q</I><SUB><I>a</I></SUB>, <I>q</I><SUB><I>b</I></SUB>}>
  ];

  qb [
    label=<{<I>q</I><SUB><I>b</I></SUB>}>
  ];

  q1 [
    label=<{<I>q</I><SUB><I>1</I></SUB>}>,
    shape=doublecircle
  ];

  empty [
    label="∅"
  ];

  start:e -> q0a:w;

  q0a -> qab [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  q0a -> qb  [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  q0a -> empty [label=<<I>c</I>>];

  qab -> empty [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  qab -> qb    [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  qab -> q1    [label=<<I>c</I>>];

  qb -> empty [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  qb -> empty [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  qb -> q1    [label=<<I>c</I>>];

  q1 -> empty [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  q1 -> empty [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  q1 -> empty [label=<<I>c</I>>];

  empty:n -> empty:n [label=<<I>a</I>>];
  empty:e -> empty:e [label=<<I>b</I>>];
  empty:s -> empty:s [label=<<I>c</I>>];
}
```

- $K′ = 2^{K} =$ <br> $\{\varnothing,$ <br>
  $\{q_{0}\}, \{q_{a}\}, \{q_{b}\}, \{q_{1}\},$ <br>
  $\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{b}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{a}, q_{b}\}, \{q_{a}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{b}, q_{1}\},$ <br>
  $\{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{b}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{a}, q_{b}, q_{1}\},$ <br>
  $K\}$
- $Σ′ = \{a, b, c\}$
- $δ(Q, w) = Ε(⋃_{q ∈ Q}Δ(q, w))$
- $q_{0}′ = Ε(\{q_{0}\}) = \{q_{0}, q_{a}\}$
- $F′ = \{Q ∣ Q ∩ F ≠ \varnothing\} =$ <br>
  $\{\{q_{1}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{a}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{b}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{b}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{1}\}, \{q_{a}, q_{b}, q_{1}\}, K\}$

Note that the state diagram for this DFA displays only states which are *reachable* from the initial state $\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}$.
